UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


        Midcontinent Independent System                       Docket No. ER27-25-000
          Operator, Inc.


                   MOTION TO INTERVENE AND LIMITED PROTEST
                   OF SOUTHERN MINNESOTA MUNICIPAL POWER
                           AGENCY AND WPPI ENERGY

           Pursuant to Rules 211, 212, and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission’s (the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 and the

Commission’s October 2, 2026 Combined Notice of Filings #1, 2 Southern Minnesota

Municipal Power Agency (“SMMPA”) and WPPI Energy (“WPPI”) (collectively,

“Midwest TDUs”) each moves to intervene in this proceeding and together submit this

Limited Protest of Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (“MISO”) October

2, 2026 filing to revise its Open Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserve

Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish a Large Load Addition Resource Study (“LARS”)

process. 3 As MISO explains, its LARS proposal is responsive to the Commission’s June

18, 2026 Show Cause Order, 4 specifically the Commission’s preliminary finding “that

MISO’s existing Tariff may be unjust and unreasonable because it does not provide

(“MISO Filing”).

generator interconnection study procedures and services that account for the operational

dynamics of serving electrically proximate large loads.” 5

           Midwest TDUs protest one aspect of MISO’s Filing: MISO’s proposal to make

paired generation and load within the same Local Resource Zone (“Zone” or “LRZ”)

eligible for the LARS process. This geographic scope is materially different from what

the Commission contemplated in its Show Cause Order, which defined “electrically

proximate” as a large load located no more than two substations away from the

generating facility. MISO’s proposed scope is both significantly overinclusive (including

paired generation and load that may be hundreds of miles and multiple states apart) and

underinclusive (excluding pairs that may be within two or fewer substations but in

different Zones).

           Finally, Midwest TDUs appreciate that MISO’s LARS proposal requires that the

LARS Interconnection Customer remain responsible for identified Generator

Interconnection Project (“GIP”) Network Upgrades, and the LARS Associated

Transmission Customer remain responsible for any identified Baseline Reliability

Projects or Other assigned Network Upgrades. While this requirement is necessary for

LARS to be just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory, it is not sufficient. MISO

states that it intends to make a future Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 205 6 filing to

address additional cost allocation and transparency issues raised in the Show Cause

Order. The Commission should therefore condition any acceptance on MISO’s filing in

this proceeding on the Commission finding, in future proceeding(s), that MISO has

    MISO Filing, Transmittal Letter at 3 (“Transmittal Letter”) (citing Show Cause Order P 113).

satisfied its obligations with respect to the Show Cause Order’s discussion of cost

allocation and transparency as applied to LARS. Midwest TDUs reserve all rights with

respect to additional future MISO filings in response to the Show Cause Order.

I.       MOTION TO INTERVENE

         Each Midwest TDU (described in Attachment A hereto) moves to intervene with

full rights as parties to this proceeding. As market participants, load-serving entities, and

customers under MISO’s Tariff, Midwest TDUs will be directly affected by MISO’s

proposed Tariff revisions. They each have clear and substantial interests in this

proceeding that cannot be represented by any other party, and their participation would be

in the public interest. Midwest TDUs should therefore each be granted intervention.

II.        LIMITED PROTEST

           A.     MISO does not show that its proposed geographic scope for
                  paired generation and load eligible for LARS is just, reasonable,
                  and not unduly discriminatory.

           In the Show Cause Order, the Commission preliminarily found that MISO’s Tariff

appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks a generator interconnection study

process and/or generator interconnection service applicable to generation facilities

serving “electrically proximate large load[s].” 8 The Commission used the term

“electrically proximate large load” in the Show Cause Order to mean: 9

                  a large load . . . sufficiently electrically close to the
                  interconnection     customer’s      requested      point      of
                  interconnection, such that the impact on the transmission
                  system of the combination of the generating facility and the
                  load, with the exception of the transmission facilities
                  between the two, will be effectively the same as if they were
                  located at the same substation (e.g., large load that is located
                  no more than two substations away from the generating
                  facility).

When paired load and generation are located close enough such that they have the same

impact on the transmission system as if they were located at the same substation, the

Commission preliminarily found that reliance on MISO’s current generation

interconnection processes may be unjust and unreasonable because it results in

“unnecessary interconnection delays, unnecessary Network Upgrades, and an otherwise




8
    Show Cause Order P 113.
9
    Id. P 112.
                                                   -5-

inefficient expansion of the transmission system, imposing unnecessary delays and costs

on transmission customers.” 10

            In response, MISO’s proposed a new LARS process that would provide

“expedited review” to “streamline the MISO generator and load interconnection process”

for certain generation and large loads. 11 But rather than adopting the Commission’s

electrically proximate large load concept (i.e., located no more than two substations away

from the generating facility), MISO proposes that its LARS process apply to paired load

and generation located in the same Local Resource Zone (“Zone” or “LRZ”). 12 MISO’s

Filing does not come close to justifying a departing from the Show Cause Order’s

approach by substituting a geographic scope that is both overinclusive and

underinclusive.

            MISO Zones can span hundreds of miles and cross multiple states. 13 For example,

MISO Zone 1 covers parts of eastern Montana, northeast South Dakota, North Dakota,

most of Minnesota, western Wisconsin, and small portions of northeast Iowa and

northwest Illinois. As a result, MISO’s LARS filing would treat a generator in Montana

as “electrically proximate” to a large load in Wisconsin, despite the hundreds of miles

and multiple states between them. MISO fails to show that such paired generation and

load should be treated as electrically proximate, much less that they would have same

impact on the MISO Transmission System as if located at the same substation.




10
     Id. P 117.
11
     Transmittal Letter at 1.
12
     Id. at 10.
13
     See MISO Tariff, Attach. VV (Map of Local Resource Zone Boundaries).
                                             -6-

           At the same time, MISO’s proposed geographic scope for LARS excludes paired

generation and load that truly are electrically proximate. For example, under MISO’s

Filing a generator in the portion of Wisconsin covered by Zone 2 could never be treated

as electrically proximate to a large load located in the portion of Wisconsin in Zone 1,

even if they are located within two substations of each other. These pairs of generation

and load are completely denied access to the expedited LARS process, while much more

distant generation and load pairs are eligible for the limited spots available per a LARS

cycle.

           The few reasons MISO gives in support for its zonal approach to LARS are

unpersuasive and irrelevant to the Commission’s directive in the Show Cause Order. For

example, MISO states that limiting paired generation and load to a specific number of

substations—as suggested in the Show Cause Order—“could limit how MISO may

optimize common transmission solutions.”14 MISO does not explain how more distant

paired generation and load, or excluding paired generation and load close to each other

but in different Zones, will lead to more optimal transmission solutions. Nor does MISO

explain how this scope aligns with the Show Cause Order’s aim of identifying generation

and load sufficiently close to each other such that they impact the transmission system as

if they were located at the same substation.

           Moreover, MISO’s LARS construct already contains numerous elements that

broaden the scope of what should be a streamlined study process, e.g.:




14
     Transmittal Letter at 21.
                                                     -7-

            •     allowing generation at multiple Points of Interconnection for a single LARS
                  Associated Load, with separate Applications for each Point of
                  Interconnection;

            •     conducting serial studies, even when there are multiple pairs of generation and
                  load in the same Zone and even for multiple Points of Interconnection for the
                  same LARS Associated Load;

            •     permitting generation to receive Network Resource Interconnection Service
                  (“NRIS”) for up to 150% of the LARS Associated Load’s peak demand; and

            •     permitting a LARS Generating Facility to retain NRIS for up to a year without
                  its paired LARS Associated Load. 15

LARS’ flawed geographic and study scope puts in doubt the optimality of the resulting

transmission solutions that the LARS process will identify. The purpose of LARS and the

Show Cause Order’s discussion of electrically proximate large loads is to identify those

pairs of load and generation that can be studied “efficiently and effectively.” 16 A

geographic measure of eligibility for LARS that fails to address electrical proximity,

however, is incompatible with that goal.

            MISO also states that its zonal scope “avoids potential capacity import / capacity

export limitations for the individual LRZ and also avoids price separation between the

paired generation and LARS Associated Load,” 17 referring to Planning Resource Auction




15
   Under MISO’s proposal, termination of the LLGIA is triggered if “the LARS Associated Load or a
portion of the LARS Associated Load has ceased use of Transmission Service granted through LARS for a
period of one year beginning with the last date of use of such Transmission Service.” Id. at 41 (quoting
revised Article 2.3.1 of MISO Filing, Tab A, Attach. X – Appendix 6 (emphasis added)). After that full
year where there can be no associated load, MISO will then provide the generator an additional full year
“to continue to operate under the LLGIA in order to provide time for the Interconnection Customer to enter
the DPP and obtain new NR Interconnection Service,” with operations subject to MISO’s Quarterly
Operating Limits and Annual ERIS process during this one-year transition period. Id. at 17.
16
     Id. at 18.
17
     MISO Filing, Tab C, Prepared Direct Testimony of Christina Drake at 40.
                                                  -8-

capacity prices that are set by Zone under MISO’s Resource Adequacy construct. 18 These

cursory references to capacity prices are a non sequitur. MISO does not explain why the

geographic scope used for certain Resource Adequacy purposes is the correct scope for

an expedited interconnection study process. MISO also does not explain why a desire to

avoid capacity price separation should determine the geographic scope of LARS,

particularly given that there can be energy price separation (based on nodes) within the

same Zone.

        Consistent with the Show Cause Order, the scope of LARS eligibility should

instead be based on which paired generation and load are likely to either have limited

impacts on the Transmission System or result in more optimal transmission solutions

when paired, such that a unique, expedited study process is justified. An inappropriately

broad geographic scope for LARS will likely capture more generation and load pairs,

requiring more time and resources to implement, which risks detracting from MISO’s

ability to improve the timing and processes for its “standard” interconnection processes.

It also invites gaming by those seeking to take advantage of differences in the LARS and

standard generation and load interconnection study processes. In contrast, a more targeted

scope ensures that LARS is appropriately focused on generation and load pairs likely to

either present fewer challenges to the Transmission System or result in more optimal

transmission solutions when paired—without diverting more resources than necessary




 See also Transmittal Letter at 10 (stating that MISO’s proposed geographic scope for LARS “aligns with
18

MISO’s Resource Adequacy construct” and “provid[es] an incentive for Load to bring Generation in a
manner that maximizes the positive impact this Generation has on Resource Adequacy”).
                                                     -9-

away from the standard generation and load interconnection study processes that non-

paired MISO loads must depend on for affordable and reliable electricity.

            B.     Additional cost allocation issues must be addressed in future
                   proceedings.

            Under MISO’s LARS Filing, “[t]he Interconnection Customer remains

responsible for any identified GIP Network Upgrades and the LARS Associated

Transmission Customer remains responsible for any identified [Baseline Reliability

Projects] or Other assigned Network Upgrades.” 19 Midwest TDUs support this

requirement, which appropriately links cost responsibility with cost causation.

            MISO’s filing, however, does not purport to address all cost-related issues raised

in the Commission’s Show Cause Order. 20 MISO specifically notes that it is “continuing

to work with stakeholders . . . to develop the pro forma cost shifting agreement and any

necessary terms for transmission service for large loads, all of which will be submitted to

the Commission in a FPA section 205 filing by November 16, 2026.” 21 Although MISO

states that “[t]he LARS structure is compatible with these agreements and MISO will

incorporate them into LARS once they are accepted,” it also states that “LARS can be

implemented based on the Tariff revisions filed herein and need not await these future

filings.” 22




19
     Id. at 16.
20
   MISO explains that its LARS filing “responds to concerns identified in the Show Cause order regarding
proximity between large loads and their associated generation,” id. at 18, and that “other concerns raised by
the Show Cause Order . . . will ultimately be presented to the Commission in separate FPA section 205
filings by November 16, 2026,” id. at 20.
21
     Id. at 14.
22
     Id. n.66.
                                            - 10 -

       As a result, the Commission currently has an incomplete picture of how cost

allocation and transparency will work in the context of the LARS process. Midwest

TDUs do not oppose MISO responding to the Show Cause Order through multiple

section 205 filings, but the Commission must ensure that the end results are Tariff

revisions that work together and comprehensively address the issues raised in the Show

Cause Order. The Commission should therefore condition any acceptance on MISO’s

filing in this proceeding on the Commission finding, in future proceeding(s), that MISO

has satisfied its obligations with respect to the Show Cause Order’s discussion of cost

allocation and transparency as applied to LARS.

                                     CONCLUSION

       For the reasons discussed above, the Commission should (1) reject MISO’s

proposed geographic scope for paired generation and load eligible for LARS and direct

MISO to revise its Tariff language consistent with the Show Cause Order; and

(2) condition any acceptance on MISO’s filing in this proceeding on the Commission

finding, in future proceeding(s), that MISO has satisfied its obligations with respect to the

Show Cause Order’s discussion of cost allocation and transparency as applied to LARS.

              ATTACHMENT A: DESCRIPTION OF MIDWEST TDUS



       Southern Minnesota Municipal Power Agency (“SMMPA”) is a joint action

agency composed of seventeen member municipalities in Minnesota that own and operate

municipal electric systems. SMMPA is also a non-profit political subdivision of the State

of Minnesota organized under Chapter 453 of the Minnesota Statutes that is not subject to

the Commission’s full jurisdiction. SMMPA became a Transmission Owning Member of

MISO, effective April 1, 2006.

       WPPI Energy (“WPPI”) is a municipal electric company formed pursuant to

Wis. Stat. § 66.0825. WPPI provides bulk power and other services to its 51 members (50

municipalities and one cooperative), each of which operates a distribution utility and sells

electricity at retail to the residences, businesses, and industries in and around its

municipality. These members are located within the Wisconsin, Michigan, and/or Iowa

service territories of four large investor-owned utilities: Northern States Power-

Wisconsin (Xcel Energy (“Xcel”)), WEC Energy Group (Wisconsin Electric Power

Company (“WEPCO”) and Wisconsin Public Service Corp. (“WPS”)), Upper Peninsula

Power Co., and Alliant Energy (Wisconsin Power & Light Co. (“WP&L”) and Interstate

Power and Light Co.). The bulk of WPPI’s load is on the American Transmission

Company LLC (“ATCLLC”), Xcel, or ITC Midwest transmission systems, although

some of WPPI’s resources are located in other transmission zones in MISO, as well as in

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. WPPI supplies the bulk power and energy requirements of

its members from generation resources owned by WPPI and through purchased power

contracts.

       WPPI is a longstanding member of MISO, with both generation and load within

the MISO footprint, and owns portions of transmission projects. WPPI also is a

participating owner of ATCLLC, a MISO Transmission Owner which was formed

pursuant to 1999 Wisconsin Act 9 with WPPI’s support.
